title: Seventy times seven
hookLine: Peter asks: seven times? Jesus: seventy times seven (Matthew 18:21–22)
carry: a number too big to keep track of

cards: How many times is enough? Ask it about the roommate who leaves the dishes, again, or the coworker who takes credit in the meeting, says sorry after, and does it the next week. The first time, letting it go feels generous.
The third time it feels foolish. Somewhere around there, a reasonable person starts asking where the line is.
Peter, one of Jesus's closest followers, asked exactly that, out loud, and even offered a number that sounds generous. Today: seventy times seven.

teach.b: First, the question. Matthew tells it in two short verses. In the King James words, Peter asks: "Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?"
Not a stranger: my brother, someone close, who will keep showing up. And Peter's number isn't stingy. Seven times is a lot of patience with one person.
Second, the answer. Jesus says: "I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." Some readers take the Greek as seventy times seven, others as seventy-seven times.

teach.h: A NUMBER TOO BIG TO COUNT.
teach.b: Either way, it isn't a bigger number to count up to. It's a number too big to keep track of. The answer quietly takes the counting away.

Luke's Gospel has a version that is even more domestic: "if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him." Seven times in one day.
Not a betrayal once a decade: ordinary life, with someone you live alongside. Fourth, what it doesn't say. It doesn't tell Peter to pretend nothing happened.
In Matthew, the verses just before lay out how to go to a brother who has wronged you and speak to him directly.

teach.h: NAME IT, BUT STOP THE TALLY.
teach.b: Some Christian teachers read the two together: you can name the wrong, set a limit, even keep your distance, and still refuse to keep a running total in your heart.
Forgiveness, in this reading, is about the count kept inside, not about letting harm continue.

how: Christian teachers turn to Matthew 18:21–22 when speaking about forgiveness in families and congregations, and preachers sometimes pair it with the verses just before it on going to the person who wronged you.

the disciple who asked Jesus how often to forgive
the disciple who betrayed Jesus for silver

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.

s: Peter's offer of seven times was stingy
seven times is a lot of patience; the answer simply takes the counting away.
Luke's version imagines being wronged seven times in a single day
"seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent."
the passage says to pretend nothing happened
the verses just before it describe going to the person and naming the wrong.

games.q: you're Peter. your brother keeps wronging you, and you want to be generous. what number do you offer Jesus?
o: as many as it takes, no limit.
games.why: Peter offers seven, which is already patient. the answer, seventy times seven, makes the counting itself the problem.

practice: Picture one thing someone close to you does again and again, nothing dangerous, just something that wears on you, and notice the little counter in your head: the fifth time, the tenth.
Set the counter down; you can still think it's wrong and still plan to talk about it, and each time the tally comes back, breathe out and set it down again.
If you pray, you can name that person once more, without a number attached.

wordCard.voice: Peter. The disciple who asked Jesus how often to forgive, and got an answer too big to keep count. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 18:22: some read seventy times seven, some seventy-seven times.

carryVoice: Your line: a number too big to keep track of. Name the wrong, and let the tally go. See you tomorrow.
